title: Metadata API & SEO (generateMetadata, OG, sitemap)
summary: The App Router's **Metadata API** lets you set `<title>`, descriptions, Open Graph, Twitter cards, and canonical URLs by exporting a static `metadata` object or an async **`generateMetadata`** function — and because Next renders these on the server (SSR/SSG), crawlers see real tags. File conventions like **`sitemap.ts`** and **`robots.ts`** round out technical SEO.

subtopics.title: Static metadata export
subtopics.explanation: Export a `metadata` object from a `layout.tsx` or `page.tsx` and Next renders the corresponding `<head>` tags on the server. It's typed (`Metadata`), merges down the route tree, and is the simplest way to set a page's title, description, and social tags when they don't depend on data.
subtopics.example:
import type { Metadata } from 'next';
export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Pricing', description: 'Our plans' };

subtopics.title: generateMetadata (dynamic)
subtopics.explanation: When metadata depends on data — a product name, a blog post title — export an async `generateMetadata({ params })` function instead of a static object. It runs on the server, can `await fetch`, and returns the same `Metadata` shape. Next dedupes fetches shared with the page so you don't fetch twice.

subtopics.title: Title templates
subtopics.explanation: Set `title.template` in a layout (e.g. `'%s | Acme'`) and child pages provide only the `%s` part via `title.default` or a plain string. This gives consistent, brand-suffixed titles across the site without repeating the brand on every page. Use `title.absolute` to opt out of the template.

subtopics.title: Open Graph & Twitter cards
subtopics.explanation: The `openGraph` and `twitter` fields control how links look when shared on social platforms — title, description, and preview image. Next emits the right `og:` and `twitter:` meta tags. You can also generate dynamic preview images with the `opengraph-image` file convention.

subtopics.title: sitemap.ts & robots.ts
subtopics.explanation: Add `app/sitemap.ts` exporting a default function that returns a list of URLs (with optional lastModified/priority), and `app/robots.ts` returning crawl rules. Next serves them at `/sitemap.xml` and `/robots.txt`. They can be dynamic — e.g. enumerate all product slugs from the database.

subtopics.title: Canonical URLs
subtopics.explanation: Set `alternates.canonical` to tell search engines the authoritative URL for a page, preventing duplicate-content penalties when the same content is reachable via multiple paths (query params, trailing slashes, www vs non-www).

foundations.overview: Next.js replaces hand-managed <head> tags and react-helmet-style libraries with a typed, server-rendered Metadata API. You declare metadata as a static `metadata` export or a dynamic async `generateMetadata` function, and Next emits the correct head tags on the server. Paired with file conventions (sitemap.ts, robots.ts, opengraph-image), it covers most technical SEO out of the box.
foundations.formalDefinition: The Metadata API is a set of exports (`metadata: Metadata` or `generateMetadata(): Promise<Metadata>`) from layouts/pages that Next.js resolves on the server and merges down the route tree to produce <head> tags, plus file-based conventions (sitemap.ts, robots.ts, opengraph-image/icon files) for site-level SEO assets.
foundations.whyItMatters: Search rankings and social-share previews depend on correct, crawlable head tags. Because Next renders metadata on the server (SSR/SSG), crawlers and link unfurlers receive fully-formed tags without executing JS — which client-only meta-tag libraries cannot guarantee. Good metadata directly drives organic traffic and click-through.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of metadata as data that flows down the route tree and merges: a root layout sets the title template and defaults, each page overrides the `%s` slot and its description/OG. Static data → `metadata` object; data-dependent → `generateMetadata`. Site-wide concerns (sitemap, robots) are separate files at the app root.
foundations.browserPerspective: Because the tags are server-rendered, the very first HTML the browser (and any crawler) receives already contains the correct <title>, meta description, og:* and twitter:* tags — no hydration or client fetch needed for them to appear in 'view source'.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A blog uses generateMetadata to set each post's title/description/OG image from its content; a layout sets the '%s | Acme' title template; app/sitemap.ts enumerates all post slugs; app/robots.ts blocks /admin while allowing everything else.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct titles, descriptions, canonical tags, and OG images raise search rankings and social click-through, which compounds into organic acquisition — often the cheapest growth channel for content and commerce sites.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A single typed API removes ad-hoc head management and prevents subtle bugs (duplicate tags, missing OG images), while file conventions standardize sitemap/robots generation so SEO assets stay in sync with the route tree.
foundations.performanceImpact: Metadata is resolved on the server alongside the page; Next dedupes fetches shared between generateMetadata and the page so you don't pay for the same request twice, and static metadata adds no client JS.
commonUseCases: Dynamic per-page titles/descriptions from CMS or DB via generateMetadata
Brand-suffixed titles with a layout title template
Rich social previews via openGraph/twitter and opengraph-image
sitemap.ts / robots.ts for crawl discovery and rules
Canonical URLs to avoid duplicate-content issues

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can set metadata from a Client Component or with the document head at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The Metadata API only works via metadata/generateMetadata exports in Server Components (layouts/pages); Client Components can't export metadata.

commonMisconceptions.myth: SEO works the same with CSR as with SSR/SSG.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Server-rendered metadata appears in the initial HTML crawlers reliably read; client-only meta tags depend on the crawler executing JS, which is slower and less reliable.

debuggingLab.title: Why don't my meta tags show up in the page source?
debuggingLab.symptom: A product page sets its title with document.title in a useEffect, but search results and social previews show the generic site title, and 'view source' has no product title.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Setting document.title (or rendering head tags) on the client only happens after JS loads and hydration runs. Crawlers and social unfurlers read the initial server HTML, which still has the generic title — so the dynamic title never makes it into the source they index. Metadata must be produced on the server via the Metadata API.
commonMistakes: Using document.title / client-side head libraries for SEO-critical tags.
Trying to export metadata from a 'use client' component (it's ignored).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the title into a server-rendered generateMetadata so the correct tag is in the initial HTML.

theory.question: How does the Next.js Metadata API work, and what's the difference between the static metadata export and generateMetadata?
theory.directAnswer: You set metadata by exporting either a static `metadata` object (typed as `Metadata`) or an async `generateMetadata` function from a layout or page. Next resolves both on the server and merges them down the route tree into <head> tags. Use the static export when the values are known at build/compile time; use generateMetadata when they depend on data (params, fetched content) since it can await fetches. Next dedupes requests shared between generateMetadata and the page.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A server-resolved API for producing <head> tags via metadata/generateMetadata exports.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To replace fragile client-side head management with typed, crawlable, server-rendered metadata.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Exports merge down the tree; static metadata is constant, generateMetadata runs per request/build and can fetch data, returning the same Metadata shape.

theory.whyImportant: Metadata correctness drives SEO and social sharing, and the static-vs-dynamic distinction is a common App Router interview point.
theory.realWorldExample: A blog post page uses generateMetadata to set title/description/OG image from the post, while the root layout sets the title template and defaults statically.

nestedTopics.title: Merging
nestedTopics.explanation: Child metadata overrides/extends parent metadata down the route tree.

nestedTopics.title: Fetch dedupe
nestedTopics.explanation: A fetch used in both generateMetadata and the page is deduped by Next, so you don't pay twice.

followUps.question: Can a Client Component export metadata?
followUps.answer: No — metadata/generateMetadata only work in Server Components (layouts/pages); a 'use client' file's export is ignored.

followUps.question: How do title templates work?
followUps.answer: A layout sets title.template like '%s | Acme'; child pages provide the %s value, and title.absolute opts out of the template.

theory.question: Why do SSR/SSG help SEO compared to client-side rendering, and how do canonical URLs fit in?
theory.directAnswer: With SSR/SSG, the title, meta description, OG/Twitter tags, and content are in the initial HTML, so crawlers and social unfurlers reliably read them without executing JS. CSR delays those tags until JS hydrates, which crawlers may render slowly or inconsistently. Canonical URLs (set via alternates.canonical) tell search engines the authoritative URL for a page so duplicate paths — query params, trailing slashes, www variants — don't dilute ranking or trigger duplicate-content penalties.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Server-rendered metadata + content in the first HTML response, plus canonical tags for de-duplication.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Crawlers index the HTML they receive; server rendering guarantees the SEO-critical tags are present immediately.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next emits resolved head tags during SSR/SSG; alternates.canonical writes a <link rel=canonical> pointing to the preferred URL.

theory.whyImportant: It explains the SEO value proposition of Next and the role of canonical tags — both frequent interview themes.
theory.realWorldExample: A product reachable at /p/123 and /p/123?ref=email sets canonical to /p/123 so both consolidate ranking signals.

nestedTopics.title: Crawl reliability
nestedTopics.explanation: Server HTML is read directly; client-rendered tags depend on the crawler's JS rendering budget.

nestedTopics.title: Duplicate content
nestedTopics.explanation: Canonical tags consolidate signals across duplicate URLs to one authoritative page.

followUps.question: Does dynamic metadata force a route to be dynamic?
followUps.answer: Only if generateMetadata uses uncached/dynamic data; with cacheable fetches the route can still be statically generated (SSG).

scenario.question: Marketing reports that shared product links show the site logo instead of the product, and Google indexes generic titles. How do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The product pages are almost certainly setting metadata on the client or not at all. I'd implement async generateMetadata in the product page (a Server Component) to set title, description, and openGraph (including a per-product image) from the fetched product, set a canonical URL, and rely on SSR/SSG so the tags are in the initial HTML. I'd verify with 'view source' and a social-card debugger, and add a sitemap.ts enumerating product slugs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A client-side metadata problem causing missing OG/title in crawled HTML.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Client-set tags aren't in the server response crawlers and unfurlers read.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: generateMetadata produces the tags server-side, so the first HTML carries correct og:image/title.

scenario.whyImportant: Connecting a real symptom (bad previews/titles) to the server-rendered Metadata API is exactly what interviewers probe.

nestedTopics.title: Validation
nestedTopics.explanation: Use social debuggers and 'view source' to confirm server-rendered tags.

followUps.question: How would you generate a unique OG image per product?
followUps.answer: Add an opengraph-image.tsx in the route using next/og (ImageResponse) to render an image from the product data.

coding.question: Write a layout title template plus a page's generateMetadata that sets title, description, OG image, and a canonical URL from fetched data.
coding.thoughtProcess: The layout owns the title template and shared defaults. The page exports async generateMetadata that fetches the resource by params and returns title/description/openGraph/alternates. Types come from next's Metadata.
coding.lineByLine: The layout sets the title template, a default description, and metadataBase so relative URLs (OG images, canonical) resolve to absolute ones. generateMetadata fetches the product and returns title (filling the template's %s), description, openGraph with a product image, a twitter card type, and a canonical URL. The fetch is deduped with the page's own getProduct call.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — metadata resolution, not an algorithm.

alternativeApproaches.title: Static metadata
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For pages whose tags never change, export a constant metadata object instead of generateMetadata.
alternativeApproaches.code: export const metadata = { title: 'Pricing', description: 'Our plans' };

followUps.question: What does metadataBase do?
followUps.answer: It sets the base URL so relative OG/canonical paths resolve to absolute URLs in the rendered tags.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Centralize shared defaults (title template, metadataBase, base OG) in the root layout and override per page with static metadata or generateMetadata. Keep site-level SEO assets as file conventions: sitemap.ts, robots.ts, and opengraph-image for dynamic previews.
productionDeepDive.performance: Prefer static metadata where possible (zero data cost) and let cacheable generateMetadata fetches keep routes statically generated. Rely on Next's request deduping so metadata and page share one fetch; avoid uncached fetches in generateMetadata that needlessly force dynamic rendering.
productionDeepDive.security: metadataBase and canonical should point to your canonical production origin; don't leak preview/internal hostnames into OG/canonical tags. robots.ts should disallow sensitive paths (admin, internal APIs) from crawling.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Generate sitemaps dynamically (and split large ones via sitemap index) so they stay in sync as content grows. ISR/SSG keeps metadata generation off the critical request path at scale.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A typed Metadata API plus co-located generateMetadata makes SEO behavior reviewable per route. Keep the title template and defaults in one place so brand changes are a single edit.
productionDeepDive.observability: Validate tags with 'view source', Google Search Console, and social-card debuggers in CI or pre-release checks. Monitor indexing coverage and click-through to catch regressions from metadata changes.

caseStudies.company: Commerce/content sites migrating to the App Router
caseStudies.problem: Client-rendered titles/OG produced poor previews and weak indexing.
caseStudies.solution: Moved SEO tags to server-rendered generateMetadata with canonical URLs and dynamic OG images, plus dynamic sitemap.ts.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more server work per route vs. reliable, crawlable tags and better previews.
caseStudies.lessons: SEO-critical tags must be server-rendered; canonical URLs and sitemaps are not optional at scale.

interviewQuestions: Why must SEO tags be server-rendered rather than set on the client?
When do you choose generateMetadata over a static metadata export?

keyTakeaways: Set metadata via a static metadata export (constant values) or async generateMetadata (data-driven); both resolve on the server and merge down the route tree.
Server-rendered tags (SSR/SSG) put title/description/OG into the initial HTML, which crawlers and social unfurlers read reliably — unlike client-set tags.
Title templates (layout '%s | Acme') give consistent brand-suffixed titles; openGraph/twitter control social previews.
sitemap.ts and robots.ts are file conventions served at /sitemap.xml and /robots.txt and can be generated dynamically.
Canonical URLs (alternates.canonical) consolidate duplicate paths to one authoritative URL to protect rankings.
